text: Purchased a groupon with several friends to go to a Belgian beer pairing with a 5 course meal here recently. I will start by saying I am a huge beer enthusiast and know a fair amount on the subject, but I have never been to a dinner like this so I was looking forward to an evening of fun and learning. The night started with a self-guided tour of the house. If you like old historic houses this will definitely be right up your alley. It is a beautiful old home and has a very nice design, some of the modern updates do hurt the look and feel of the building though. Unfortunately this was the nicest part of the evening. After taking the tour we return to the downstairs for a beer reception. The reception consisted of about ten different beers being opened and approximately 2 ounces poured each time you passed through the line. MAYBE 1/3 of these beers were Belgian, the staff had no information or opinion on them, and they were served in whatever order they were grabbed which made tasting difficult as no water or bread was provided and going from a double chocolate stout to a blonde ruins your palette. The tasting line wound through the old house with no order, huge bottlenecks, and was served by a staff with no personality or sense of humor. After spending an hour standing to receive approximately 10 ounces of beer we were called to sit in the dining room and given a run down of the history of the house and encouraged to come to a wine pairing class. We were then told by owner Karen Glass that she didn't care for beer because it tasted terrible and their dinner was thrown together(which showed). The first course comes out and consisted of a piece of bread with cheese on it and was paired with blonde. So far so good, but unfortunately this was the best part of the meal. The beers were served in 2 ounce pours while anybody that requested wine got full pours into a bottomless glass. From the beginning they made it apparent they favored wine and even at a BEER dinner we would still be treated as second class. The second course comes out and it's a brown rice mixed with salad and vinaigrette(was someone drunk in the kitchen?) It was a horrible combination of blandness paired with a cherry ale(the ale was delicious, but again 2 ounces and you're cut off). Time for course three, muscles. The muscles were flavored well, but were served colder than my room temperature salad rice mixture and paired with more of the cherry ale(at least with a second 2 ounce pour I got to try a little more). At this point we discuss leaving, but thanks to terrific company at our table we decided to make the most of it and to stick it out. The fourth course comes out and it includes an overcooked pot roast mush mixed with salad(Really more salad?) and a shot of doppelbock. At this point we try requesting more beers and we're informed that there was wine available if we wanted something else to drink. (Thanks, I thought I paid for a BEER dinner.) And we move on to the fifth and final course of the night(Thank goodness, I can't wait to go get a pint and something that resembles food). Karen informs us that she would have liked to have served waffles(obviously this is the extent of her knowledge when it comes to Belgian food) but instead decided on an overcooked and rock hard butter cake that was no doubt left over from one of her MUCH more sophisticated wine dinners that none of us simpletons would appreciate. It was paired with a shot of raspberry lambic and we were promptly given our checks for taxes and gratuity. In summary this may be a nice place for a wine dinner(or a beer dinner where you'd rather have wine) and you don't care about the quality of food or the friendliness of the staff. For what I paid I could have had a fantastic dinner at any number of restaurants in Indy and spoken with a much more informed waiter regarding my choices in beer without having judgement passed on me. Steer clear unless you enjoy disappointment.
label: NEG

text: I have been going to Salon de Nouveau for years and have had only pleasant experiences for waxing with Alyssa. The other experiences not so much. The haircuts - two of the worst hair cuts ever! The first time, they literally cut all of my hair off. I asked for short layers, but to keep the overall length. I wore glasses at the time (if you met me pre-lasik, you know what my coke bottle bottoms looked like) and I could not see what the stylist was doing until she was like ok put your glasses on! Tada! I earned the nickname baldylocks. My shoulder length hair was not a pixie cut and there was nothing I could do about it. My hair grows really slow so this was an extremely traumatic experience. The next time was three years later, I saw a more experienced stylist who was highly recommended and honestly she made me feel so uncomfortable. She was silent the entire time. No conversation, she tugged at my hair and I had a pounding headache by the time I left. It was terrible. The mani/pedi This was more of a cuticle push with polish. There was no trimming and the manicurist was just not pleasant. It was over priced for what I received. One time was more than enough. Why did I keep going back? No, I'm not a masochist, I just couldn't understand how a place that employed my beloved aesthetician could have some many employees who were just sub par. Alyssa was this salons best kept secret-- in a sense. She wasn't a secret, but it was a pleasant surprise to any one I referred. Even those who had visiting the salon before, but never seen her for a service. She was always so nice, happy and eager to make you happy and your skin beautiful. She able to my tame my unsightly super thick, but sparse brows and make them pretty. I referred so many friends and family members to her and every single one of them was pleased. I recently called to make one of four random appointments per year and earned that she recently moved to M Salon. I'm sorry, but she was the reason I kept coming back and tried other services. I must say that it is time bid Salon Nouveau adieu for services. They do, however, sell Bumble and Bumble products, so I may see them a time or two in the future. Maybe you will have better luck, if you do, please share!

text: This theater has an open area when you walk in which provides an arcade as well as a mini restaurant. The Big D auditoriums are nice, but this theater has some very tricky price points. The IMAX, 3D movies, and Big D movies all charge you a premium to attend those movies. Our showing of Cars 2 was about 20 minutes late in seating on a Saturday afternoon. I would not expect this type of mismanagement from a larger theater during the summer months. Also, there are a significant amount of kids that frequent this theater due to the size and location. Another disadvantage is no evidence of a Fandango kiosk. The best theaters have a significant amount of marketing materials placed in premium locations through the theater. They have the ticketing outside and ample kiosks for Fandango inside and outside. I also prefer to see a large auditorium with a nice arcade, mini restaurant, play area, large and clean restrooms. The theater should be split nicely into four large auditoriums for easy access, then split into two sections off to the end. These split sections should provide access to concessions. The Franklin theater had virtually none of this design and is a poor excuse for theater management and design. Regardless, this is probably the best mainstream theater in the Nashville area. But this doesn't make it a great theater.

text: OK...first off I want to say that I am not a die hard Ice Cream fanatic like some, and it takes a lot to impress me as far as Ice Cream goes. THIS IS THE BEST ICE CREAM I HAVE EVER HAD!!! I have been here 2 times now and every time it seems to get better and better like a fine wine with age. I ordered a caramel sundae with vanilla ice cream, whipped cream, peanuts, and of course a cherry on top. Yes, both times! It seems that all of there Ice Cream and toppings are made in house with pure cane sugar and premium cream. The vanilla ice cream tasted like I was eating a vanilla pod with a touch of cream and a touch of cane sugar. The caramel was thick, sweet and a dash of salty, and the whipped cream was definitely homemade that day. On our second visit we took some out of town friends and we had a chance to see and taste some of the other specialties Franklin Fountain offers. 1 of them was a Peanut Butter Milkshake which we come to find out that they make there own PB in house. The second was a Root Beer Float that looked like the glass was 2 feet tall. Did I mention the straws were a throwback to the 20's or 30's and were not plastic but old school paper straws. The ambiance is amazing and my first thought was I just walked into the "Boardwalk Empire" era. The call the bathroom a water closet "WC" is on the door, they have marble countertops with swing out chairs. The radio was playing old time classics from the 20's and the Soda Jerks are all decked out in short sleeve button up shirts with bow ties. If you have not been here and are planning a trip to Philly or if you live close you have to go...you won't be sorry!

The portions were quite hearty according to my standards. The Fajita Tacos (what I got) were amazing. . . piping hot, yummy seitan and amazing vegan sour cream. Everyone else's food was excellent (the Kalamata hummus was fabulous, the burgers wonderful). We topped it off with a Lavender Vanilla cupcake which was outta control good. The service was excellent. The staff affirmed my faith in my personal motto: you don't have to be a freak to be a vegan. They were all funky in their own way but treated us "normal-ish" people in a very friendly manner. They even cheerfully answered our ingredient/recipe inquiries. This is our new absolute favorite restaurant. .. we can't wait to try everything on the menu.

text: What a surprise this place was. I had a large group of friends from Austin that I met up with on Frenchman. We were looking for a spot to just hang out and drink with seating and not a lot of loud noise. No such spot was to be found on Frenchman on this night. I decided to walk over to Molly's because I'm stupid and deep inside I knew Molly's would be packed. It was. Now who's stupid? Me. To my surprise, I saw Turtle Bay a few doors down and it wasn't crowded at all. We figured we would go inside and have a drink or two. I had Turtle Bay pegged as touristy, under new ownership and name, here today and gone tomorrow place. Wrong. Now who's stupid? Still me. In reality, it's a nice little spot with lots of good beers on tap. The bartender was super friendly as well. The big surprise was the courtyard in the back. This area fit our entire group and then some. We were rolling about fifteen deep because that's just how we do. Yeah, I just said that. Still stupid. We had a great time in the back and it wasn't noisy or bothersome at all. There is a kitchen cooking up late night food. I have to say, the food is surprisingly good. Pretty decent pizza. It's true. It's a nice sized menu when anything would probably do. To be fair, we were hungry and drinking, so you might want to try this out for yourself. The only downside is the parking around the Quarter. I'm not often in that area for drinks. I'm sure that adds to the annoyance of parking. Depends on the night. Anyway, Turtle Bay rescued the night and I'll probably be stopping in again. Great little place. FACTOID: They have a signature frozen drink in a neon green plastic container called the Turtle Bomb. My friend wanted a Hand Grenade and thought this was it. It was not. However, she now performs on a highly popular improv group in Austin called Hand Bomb as a tribute to our fun night at Turtle Bay.

After getting our drink order, we asked the waiter where the food menu was and were told that the blue piece of paper was the menu for the night which included a 5 course meal for two at $40 each. Once we found that out we checked out what the meal was and what choices we had and there was nothing vegetarian on it at all. My wife asked if they could possibly make something vegetarian for her and they said they couldn't. After hearing that we left and went next door to an Indian restaurant named the Curry Leaf. I really wanted to like this place as did my wife and both of us were excited to be going here for our anniversary. After our experience here we will not be going back. As I mentioned earlier I hate to give places 1 star but the only reason this place didn't get 1 star from me is because the staff was very apologetic and seemed sincere.

My point is, why hold a 'Chinese' place to a standard that it must be 'authentic' when we seem to overlook the fact that you'd be damn hard-pressed to find corned beef & cabbage on the menu in any restaurant in Ireland? It would sometimes be 5 months between visits, and Mr. Chen (OK, the owner, not sure if that's really his name), always remembered us and what we like to order. Is this some sort of Jedi mind trick? "you'll have General Tso's chicken, Crab Rangoon and fried rice.". Yes, Mr. Chen. And we'll love it! Is it health food? No. Is it authentic, probably not. Is it fresh and hot? Yes. Is it delicious? YES! So, when I started traveling, and when I'd be in town, all my friend would have to say is 'Chen?' when she'd want to invite me to meet for lunch. Yes, please! So yes, we all agree, House of Chen is probably not what you'd find in downtown Chóngqìng or in the countryside of Xinjiang. text: I LOVE RDHD!! I was only introduced to this dance fitness class less than a year ago, but I am HOOKED! (So much so, in fact, that I got the certification to teach it and sub for other instructors whenever I can.) Who will like RHDF? If you love to move or love to dance, you'll love this class. You don't have to be a pro dancer to enjoy this class--it really is for everyone, from those who only dance around their house while vacuuming (yes, I know you do it, cause I do, too!) to those who have taken dance classes since birth, practically. I took dance classes for 15 years, but there is still so much I can do to make myself feel challenged by the steps. The movements are designed so that ANYONE can do them and feel sexy, flirty, and like you're getting a great workout (which you are!) My favorite part of RHDF is the performance songs because that's when you really feel like you're starring in a musical or dancing next with Beyonce in a music video. The instructor uses one song to teach you the moves that you'll do in the performance song (which are mostly moves you do in other dances--so it's easy to catch on!), while not letting your heart rate drop. Then we go into the performance song and perform the combination of dance steps straight through a few times. Even if you've never taken a dance class before, you'll feel so confident at the end of the song when you've performed the steps several times in a row. This is what makes RHDF unique--it's the same kind of adding-on technique you might find in a step class, but it doesn't take the entire class to build the routine (which was something that always drove me batty about step--can we just move on to something different already??) Also, your heartrate doesn't drop while you're learning the moves, which makes it different from an actual dance class and ensures that you're getting a great cardio workout the whole hour. Check out www.redhotdancefitness.com and find out where you can take a class. Alison King Red Hot Dance Fitness Instructor

text: On our last night of vacation in Tucson, I chose to take my family out to Pinnacle Peak. For those folks who know Tucson, the mere mention of this place will bring smiles and some smirks. It is a place where a plain, old-fashioned steak restaurant and Old West tourist kitsch collide in an orgy of manly cuisine and severed neck-ties. The restaurant resides on the east side of Tucson off of Tanque Verde Road, in the middle of a relatively small Old West homage called Trail Dust Town. Getting over here was quite the chore, since we came from the northwest part of town and were driving during rush-hour. Businesses, both real and facades, make up this old tourist spot. For example, you might find a portrait studio in one of the buildings, but you will also find a candy shop and a shooting gallery arcade, with several photo-op spots around the town. They also run some "shoot-outs" and similar shows out in the town-circle area, and there is a kiddy-train that travels through the entire grounds. But the focal point is the restaurant that looks like an old West saloon/hotel from the outside: Pinnacle Peak. I suspect the Peak has been around for 40+ years, and with good reason. They cater to the tourist with everything you would expect a mock-up Old West town to have, and they do it in a tongue-in-cheek kind of way. For example, the waiters all have names of famous Old West persons. Ours was Bat Masterson. You'll find Wyatt Earp, Doc Holliday and their compatriots waiting on tables, too. One of the more obvious items patrons will notice (at least if you look up) are the array of half-cut neck-ties that adorn the ceiling of the restaurant. One of the Peak's claims to fame (and an in-joke for the locals taking visitors there) are these symbols to American stuffiness. They pride themselves on being a laid-back kind of place, and so if you have not already read the other reviews that have warned you, here is one more: do NOT wear a tie here unless you are looking to get rid of it. They do not make exceptions, and not everyone has left with a laugh about it. The Peak serves basic, good meat-and-potatoes kind of food, with the high point being their steaks. They are a sister restaurant to El Corral, and since we had already eaten at the Corral earlier in our stay, I decided not to go for the recommended bone-in ribeye this time. Their featured steaks are the cowboy (1.5 lbs of T-bone), the cowgirl (1 lb. T-bone) and some kind of super-duper Big Cowboy steak that I didn't even want to hear described. My wife went for their big filet mignon, I chose the cowgirl (because I draw the line at 1 lb. of pure beef in one sitting), and our 4-year-old daughter got the hot dog. A couple things of which you should be aware: every table gets thick Texas bread slices with butter and the dinner comes with a big bowl of baked beans. The dinners also typically come with a baked potato or similar item, and a salad. The steaks are cooked on a grill using mesquite wood, which imparts a nice subtle smoky flavor. Well, by now you must realize that our entire dining experience here was simply awesome. The food was excellent, as was the service. The steaks were cooked just right. Bat kept coming to check on us, and even provided us with a free bowl of cooked mushrooms to try with our steaks. I must also add that I am not a baked beans fan, but the baked beans here were wonderful. I wish I had more room to eat them. The salad, bread and other accoutrements were fine but nothing special. And how about a balloon sculptor who can twist colored balloons into a turtle! Try finding that on your next trip to Chucky Cheese. I don't know what more I can say other than this was a great place to cap off our stay in Tucson. My family enjoyed it and it brought back some good memories for me from when I lived here 20 years ago. Even if you are not into Old West kitsch, I think you'll still enjoy Pinnacle Peak.

After studying the menu for an embarrassingly long time (it's not that I didn't know what I wanted to order, I just wanted too many things), I ordered the arugula salad with pine nuts and parmigiano to start. For my entree I had the lobster risotto. Friggin' amazing! Be warned, the risotto is dense and they don't skimp on the portions here, so after a few bites I was entirely stuffed. There were large pieces of lobster in the risotto and small pieces of asparagus. It was cooked just right: not overcooked but enough so that starches were released from the arborio rice resulting in pure creamy deliciousness! I also tasted a bite of my friend's filet mignon and scalloped potatoes. I am not even a red meat eater and I am pretty sure that was one of the greatest pieces of meat I have ever tasted. Potatoes were equally delicious. We had to skip out on dessert, after a full bottle of wine and all that food we couldn't squeeze it in. Will definitely be back soon to try out some of the other entrees.

text: So far YoGo is a NoGo for me. I was really excited to see a frozen yogurt shop opening up in my neighbourhood. I was especially excited, since I have recently visited New York, where froyo is all-the-rage. And I think it's great that this self-serve concept is being introduced into Edmonton. They let you try the flavours in tiny sample cups. My very first taste was vanilla, which was a major disappointment. The one flavour that should taste the most plain, tasted the worst. It was very strong, very fake, and very sweet; not to mention, the consistency was thin and seemed watered-down. I tried some of the other flavours, like blueberry and mango, which tasted better, but they are so strong and sweet that I don't think I'd want to have more than a sample-sized cup. The pricing confuses me. It's expensive, but it would be well-justified if the yogurt was of higher quality. This is a specialized shop charging specialized prices for something that tastes like it's being pumped out of a machine at the local 7-11. For a place like this, I expect a high-quality, thick and creamy yogurt--lightly flavoured and lightly sweetened. If anyone wants sugar, that can all be dumped on at the toppings station. The quality and wide-selection of the toppings, however, is impressive. The fruit was very fresh. There are Mini-Eggs, which is totally awesome and lots of neat candies. The nuts are also in separate containers, which is perfect for allergies. The contrast between the Japanese-style logo and faux-upscale decor is a little weird, but if the yogurt was actually good, I probably wouldn't be mentioning this at all. I'd come here at least a few times a week, especially because of their late hours, but unless the quality of the yogurt drastically improves, I probably won't be back. I do hope it gets better though, this neighbourhood needs some good froyo!

text: I guess when you get to the point where you are the Duke or Duchess of a business, you should review them. Let me say that all of my yelp check in's at Sam's have been sitting waiting at the fuel pump for my car to fill up. If you live in Franklin, this is the cheapest place to buy gas, so I'm here at least weekly. It's reality when you live here and work in Nashville. And what else are you going to do waiting for the "click?" We do shop at Sam's in the store frequently, hubby usually does that part - and they do have some deals. I understand one other yelper's comments about how they used to be REALLY cheap, and now not so much. But to that point I say, the world is a smaller place. The purchasing in quantity idea, not as prevalent anymore. I've always known that it was cheaper to purchase soft drinks by the case at the grocery - Pepsi and Coke strongly incentivize that. We buy our "household" products (detergents, paper towels, etc.) here because it is at least as cheap as buying on sale at the grocery, and I don't have to worry about running out of TP with guests in the house. For my everyday lotion, Sam's is significantly cheaper than the grocery, Walgreen's, or Target... and for generic drugs you take every day - definitely check them out. Is Sam's cheaper than Costco? I don't know. Our family business buys a Sam's merchandise, we use Discover, so that's our choice. If you are an American Express person or debit card-er, and maybe you live closer to Costco, then go there. I have purchased several GREAT deals finding out of season merchandise (or about to be out of season) here, so when you are searching for patio furniture, holiday items, etc. - don't overlook them. Also store displays you can really negotiate hefty discounts for blemishes, etc. As I look around our house - our patio set (10 pieces, we have a large deck), dining table and six chair set, and an upholestered recliner have all come from there. So yes, I'd say we're a fan.

text: I attended Sierra Tucson in September of 2009. I have to admit that as a person who is alcoholic the last thing I wanted to do was receive treatment for an addiction I didn't think I had. But an unfortunate series of events led me to Sierra Tucson and I'm glad it did. Upon getting to Sierra Tucson, not only was I in denial about my alcohol addiction, but I was resentful, apathetic and frankly didn't want anything to do with recovery, counselors or sobriety. What I found at Sierra Tucson was the real me. The 30 days I spent in rehab was more about discovery than anything else. It was the beginning of my recovery which I still practice today. It wasn't easy and I don't think it was supposed to be. My team counselor had me examine my behaviors and patterns of thinking which led me there. What I discovered changed my life forever. The team at Sierra Tucson helped me start a process which replaced shame and guilt, as the result of trauma and alcoholism, with understanding and compassion. My wife and brother attended family week. This week helped my family and I understand how my addiction affected everyone around me, especially the ones who loved me most. This precious week also started a process of repairing the relationships I damaged as the result of my drinking. Sierra Tucson also counseled my family and led them in the direction of recovery as well. Their experiential therapy was very diverse and was beneficial for me. The nurses were not only there to dispense medication, but were there to lend an ear when I was down and in a bad place. When I left Sierra Tucson I was able to understand a little more clearly what drove me to this destructive behavior. I live life today free of alcohol and am still in recovery. If anyone is thinking of attending Sierra Tucson I would advise that all it takes to make the most of their stay is open mindedness, willingness and honesty. There is hope out there and the staff of Sierra Tucson truly understands. If you are suffering from addiction then I would recommend Sierra Tucson as the starting point to your recovery. My family and I are truly grateful to Sierra Tucson and their Alumni Group for bringing hope in time of discord.

text: Really like the classes, reallyl like the instructors and even the new (fairly) studio location is pretty cool. My main problem is they so great that others are discovering this yoga gem and classes are commonly overfilled, making postures sometimes uncomfortable and really spoiling my yoga "zen" time. Groupon has obviously given them a lot of new business and even though my husband and I would sign up for classes online (as instructed and told was necessary to be present in class) extra people would show up before us (we always got there at least 10 minutes before class) and after us who had not registered and would be admitted to class because instructors are kind and lenient on the sign up rules. I came into one class on a Sunday and actually had to turn around because people kept flowing in. We were assured that leaving (because we felt uncomfortable with so many people in the tight area) would not result in a "charged" class. We found out that was not the case because they counted us as a no show because we had signed up online for the class and chose not to stay because of overcrowding. Ridiculous. D's is blowing up because they give a great service but they really need to improve their business end now that they have grown.

text: I decided to give this joint a second chance. The first time I visited, it was late and all I tried were the beers. The porter was mediocre at best. A friend of mine lives nearby, saw something in the paper about the place, and wanted to try it. So I reserved judgment and thought "Maybe the food is better than the beer". Boy was I wrong. I tried the Shepherd's Pie, thinking that if this place portends to be an English pub, at least the Shepherd's Pie or Fish & Chips would be decent. First of all, it was tiny. They serve it in a soup bowl (the kind that you usually see French Onion soup in). All the vegetables in the pie were canned and there were green beans (!) in it. I could have rated it "mediocre" instead of "bad" if the mashed potatoes were at least lukewarm instead of stone cold. If you think I'm being harsh, my friend order the Daily (Not So) Special, which happened to be a burrito with either beef or chicken. He asked for the chicken, but received a beef burrito instead. The meat was so dry and overcooked that he ate about half of it before he realized they sent out the wrong dish. He also said the rice was cold and the beans were bland. When the server asked if everything was alright, he told her it was the worst burrito he had ever had (which surprised me because even if his food is terrible, he never says anything other than "everything is great, thanks"). I could tell he was still hungry so we ordered some wings as hot as they could make them (nuclear). They were much better than our entrees (talk about setting the bar low) and we scarfed them down. We sat and had a few beers and they were not as bad as the first time I tried them. I had the Cream-Mel (their version of Miller Lite), the Scottish Ale, and one other which was so forgettable that I don't even remember what it was. The beers are average at best -- something any homebrewer can make on their stove. The decor is pretty bland (no real theme at all), although they have a pretty nice shaded patio in front facing Highway 267. You can also see all their brewing equipment which is in the middle of the building behind glass. Service is pretty vapid which is to be expected considering all they did was hire a bunch of local college-age girls. I won't be returning to Three Pints anytime soon as there is a much better (food beer, atmosphere) brewpub right across the street.
label: NEG

text: Not a regular hot dog fan, but I love the Sonoran hot dogs! The grilled veggies that go with them are amazing too, as is the chicken torta on the regular menu. Great selection of salsas at the salsa bar, and REAL sugar soda!!

text: We should've just stuck with our first instincts to go for burgers and tater tots, but we decided to try The Gumbo Pot instead. BIG MISTAKE! First, we waited for the maitre'd, but there was no one around, so we made our way towards the interior of the restaurant only to be flagged back outside by the maitre'd. After we were seated at our table, I had to go to the ladies room. It was disgusting! The last stall was NOT clean and I almost threw up! I came back to the table where there were five of us dining. We started off with water while we decided what drinks to order. One friend ordered a SoCo Hurricane and another one ordered a Malibu Rum Punch. They each took one sip of their drinks and said they tasted wrong and were disgusting. When our waiter, Jeremy, came by to ask how things were, my friends had told him about the drinks, that they weren't any good and were thinking about ordering something else. Instead of insisting on taking those drinks away, he tried to defend the drinks and the bartender by saying that "that's how those drinks are supposed to taste. They're stronger than regular drinks." Just before he walked away, he just left the drinks sitting there. The seafood gumbo arrived and my friend and I were excited because it looked so good. Actually, it was the worst gumbo I've ever had. I was so disappointed, that I didn't finish mine. I ordered crab cakes as my entree and they were so bad too!! They were BURNT, not crispy! They were the saltiest crab cakes ever. Overall, the whole entire experience was just terrible. The ambiance was terrible. The service was awful, awful, awful!! The food was so bad!! My friends and I were just so upset that for a restaurant which charges so much $$ for their meals, they should've been more accommodating. text: After reading the glowing reviews of Big Bowl, I HAD to try it. Since I don't typically shop at Dierbergs, I didn't realize the place even existed! I stopped by on a Friday evening after work. When you walk into Dierberg's, it's right near the front of the store. They have a pretty nice selection of items. I went with the Sesame Chicken bowl, which comes with your choice of brown rice or fried rice. I went with brown rice. I also ordered chicken potstickers and crab rangoon. When I made my way to the front to pay, I noticed the selection of ginger ales. I LOVE ginger. The spicy kick of it makes me happy. So I picked up a regular ginger ale (they also had a hibiscus flavor). The sesame chicken was AMAZING for fast-Thai. The flavor was fantastic, and I loved it paired with the brown rice. The potstickers and crab rangoon? I wasn't a huge fan of either one, and only had one of each before I decided to focus my efforts on my sesame chicken. Priorities! However, the star of the show for me was the DELICIOUS ginger ale. It actually had pieces of ginger floating around, and unlike other ginger ales I've tasted, the ginger flavor was VERY pronounced. So spicy and delicious! I loved it. Prices were reasonable. I could definitely see myself coming here for a quick dinner.

text: My wife and I were looking for a clean, comfortable, economical place to stay in NOLA and based on the previous two Yelp reviews we chose the Sunburst. It was a great choice! Not perfect, but met our expectations quite nicely. We stayed there for six nights and got to know the neighborhood. We weren't as enamored with the neighborhood as previous reviewers but it was OK. It seemed a little dicey at first but felt more comfortable as the days passed. Walking distance to the Bourbon street night life is about 20 minutes. However the more enjoyable (to us) Frenchman Street club, bar and restaurant scene is less than ten minutes of walking where we heard some great music and enjoyed some really good NOLA cuisine. The Sunburst is great! We stayed in one of the smaller rooms the first night and after returning from a cruise to the Yucatan we stayed in the much larger downstairs room for five nights. The house is a ca 1900 house that is really charming in all respects. Glen and Darrell were most accommodating. No need to comment on the amenities as they were noted in previous reviews and I would concur with them. My only complaint about the large downstairs room(s) is that it is dark! Not much light comes through the front and side windows and the antique lighting doesn't provide quite enough light to read comfortably in the living room area. We rented a car on our last three days and were able to always find a parking spot right in front of the Sunburst. By the way, don't try to drive in the Canal Street/French Quarter/Downtown it's an exercise in futility. Take a cab/bus or walk. All in all, a great place to stay while visiting the Big Easy and the price is really good too.

text: Ok so I've never been a huge fan of red lobster but I was really hoping this time would change my mind.. I went with a craving for Seafood and my boyfriend. We were sat in under 10 minutes despite the seemingly large crowd of families waiting for tables. Ok so we had to wait way too long for the server to bring us our drinks and it seemed like he forgot our biscuits but the appetizers were very good! We had the lobster and crAb stuffed mushrooms and the lobster and artichoke seafood dip which had huge pieces of lobster and was pretty true to the picture on the menu. Extremely filling and delicious! Then the entree comes.. And I remember why I don't like red lobster. We ordered the lobster lovers dream to share with a side of the shrimp and lobster Mac and cheese. The Maine lobster was without a doubt overlooked it was tough and dry and the langostino lobster was questionable undercooked.. We definitely should have stopped at the appetizers.. Bottom line.. Service was subpar and food was.. Eh. Heres my recommendation.. If you really want seafood and there's nowhere else around then stop at red lobster for lunch. text: Had to get my dog's hair did, so I decided to try this place out because of it's location and cute name. The haircut was nicely done and my dog didn't seem traumatized afterwards. She even recommended that before I buy it, I let him smell the unpackaged, larger antlers just to be sure he liked them. She also gave tips on how to boil the antler if my dog should grow bored with it. I appreciated that effort and candor, since most people seem preoccupied with the sell rather than customer (human or dog) satisfaction. In fact, I found that all the staff on hand were very friendly and cheerful. This is a huge improvement from most other pet stores I've been to. I thought that the prices of items were a little high, but not exorbitant. Actually, the small collars turned out to be cheaper than what I can find at PetSmart, and the designs were unique. They also have a sizable collection of those Euro Stickers, designed for dog lovers, which I've always admired but never come across. We picked one of those up, too. I visited around Mardi Gras season, just as they were unpacking a shipment of Mardi Gras dog costumes. This is great because Soulard celebrates Mardi Gras HARD and they're smart to extend the celebration to the neighborhood's pets. I'll probably visit Pets in the City again.

text: My girlfriend and I went to this non-traditional South Philly italian spot on a Wednesday night during a Savored featuring. We were immediately greeted by a very nice man who we later learned is the owner. There were 3 or 4 other tables eating, but the crowd seemed appropriate for a weeknight. The decor is somewhat generic-modern, but it feels good. There are a few standout pieces like the wood and pipes on the wall, and the overhead lights. It certainly doesn't scream "italian," but the food did that. We started out with two appetizers (buffalo mozzarella bruschetta and chicken liver crostini) that were presented very nicely and tasted just as good. Our entrees, the linguini shrimp and lasagna, were full of flavor. Although normally a relatively plain dish, the shrimp had a great lemon cream sauce and the shrimp and pasta were cooked perfectly. The bolognese of the lasagna was very flavorful and delicious, and not oilly as many lasagnas are. In terms of the food, we had two small disappointments. Firstly, although the bread was good, it was presented with cold butter in the plastic packets, which was surprising for an otherwise nice restaurant. The second was the creme brulee dessert. Although it had a very nice flavor, the bottom half of it (served in a bowl) was cold. It seemed as if it had been pulled out of a refrigerator and the sugar was thrown on and torched, warming only the top. The chill hid what was a nice flavor. The prices were reasonable and the service was excellent. Owner Tommy was very helpful and very friendly. Although the restaurant is unique in South Philly in that it has a non-traditional, small menu and modern decor, the staff provides the friendly feel of a traditional spot. Despite a couple of small hiccups, Chiarella's is a great eatery that we look forward to enjoying again.
label: POS

text: Went here for a taste test, looking for a workplace party site. The location is good, and there is a nice variety of rooms and areas to choose from if you are looking to host an event. But we won't be having a party here. Here's what we got: Eggplant Sticks--good and fairly crisp. The remoulade sauce was pretty tasty. Crabcake Appetizer--Drunk at 4am, these would be delicious. Not drunk, they didn't taste any more special than something from the frozen food section at your local grocery. Gumbo--I'm not a gumbo fan, but it was edible. Blackened Shrimp Salad--the blackening seasoning used on the shrimp was super salty, but pretty good. The shrimp had a nice texture, and my taste test companion said the Cesar dressing was delicious. Fried Catfish w/french fries and Hushpuppies--Catfish with breading were chewy. Tartar sauce was disgusting--warm with a funky after taste. French fries were something you could definitely buy in the frozen foods section at the local grocery. Hushpuppies were so hard throughout they might have been fried yesterday. There is a fine line between attentive service and stalking. The waitstaff and managers hovered. I worry when restaurants do this, because it makes me think they are trying to see if they've gotten away with serving subpar food. My gastrointestinal tract felt dirty inside after eating here. All the fried food didn't help, but, done well, I wouldn't have cared about what we ate. Unfortunately, nothing was worth the calories.

text: 4.25 stars. Monell's is exactly what makes the South so special to those of us who have lived in the area for any tangible amount of time. Are you looking for a special treat? Look no further than the beautiful mansion at Monell's for some of the best breakfast you will find this side of the Mississippi. You are led to a lengthy table in a Southern-formal room where you eat family style with other patrons. They start you off light with a plate of biscuits, but you have the option of making them quite heavy with a think and creamy peppery white gravy that hearkens back to a time when nutritional labels had no bearing in cooking. After the biscuits and gravy, we were treated to a number of different carbohydrates - the corn pudding that everyone mentions is quite divine but I wasn't too thrilled with the cheese grits here. What was exceptionally well prepared on the carbohydrate plate were the homestyle potatoes and the sweet apples. I had to have second helpings of both of those items. Next, we were treated to a big plate of sausage, bacon, and country ham with the sausage and country ham both exceptionally prepared (the sausage squirts all over the place - it's that juicy - and the country ham has an impressive sweet finish). However, if you are at Monell's, you are saving room for the fried chicken. Monell's does a fantastic job with this decidedly Southern dish with an absolutely perfect crunch for each piece. Sadly, I could only eat one piece given all the food I had eaten during the sitting. If you want an impressive Southern meal at a very reasonable price, Monell's is a great bet. My mouth is salivating just thinking about my next visit.

text: It must be that all of the folks hired to work here have never worked at a restaurant located in an airport. If they had, they would recognize that many airport travelers do not have an overabundance of time. My travel into Indianapolis was to deliver puppies to be trained as service dogs. On completing my assignment, I was at loose ends for about 90 minutes. 11 AM, not too early for lunch, and now that I was free of dogs, I could go in, sit down and have a bite to eat. Champps Americana was only 2 gates down, so I walked up to the wait stand and asked to be seated. Greeter seated me and said my waitress would be along shortly. About a minute later, Waitress appeared. She tossed a menu on the table, looked back at the bar/kitchen area and hollered "I'll be right there". She asked me what I wanted to drink, and as she walked away, she said she would be back shortly with my water. I turned and looked at the menu. Time passed. I read about everything they serve and made my decision. Looking at my watch, it had been 5 minutes since waitress had taken my drink order. The restaurant had 4 tables seated and about 10 people sitting at the bar. I would guesstimate 20 tables total and room around the bar for another 30 people. I looked at all of the televisions I could see, although the hiphop music that was being played was too loud to hear any of the televisions. Looking again at my watch, 10 minutes had passed. Waitress appeared, put my water on the table pulled her pen out of her hair, and asked what I wanted to order. I ordered the mozzerella sticks. Waitress said, "Is that all?" When I replied it was, she gave a gusty sigh and told me it should be about 8 minutes for my order. She poked the pen back into her hair and walked away. I drank water and logged into my Kindle to get caught up on email and news. Having been on planes for the previous 12 hours (Phoenix/Denver/Charlotte/Indianapolis), I was thirsty. It took me about 5 minutes to drain the 16 ounce glass that I had been given. Waitress appeared at the table about 8 minutes after she had left previously. She delivered my mozzerella sticks and asked if I needed anything else. I asked for more water and she said she would bring some more. $7.89 before tax brought me 8 mozzerella sticks and a 2-ounce container of marinara. The cheese sticks were nothing out of the ordinary. They were well-cooked and stringy from the first to the last. The marinara, however, was very disappointing. It had a taste similar to Prego, though the tomato was not chopped as fine as a 'sauce' would be. Truth be told, I suspect the cook had combined a can of marinara sauce with a can of crushed tomato, then added some parsley for green counterpoint. The combination just did not work. On finishing my order, Waitress came by and brought my water. She did not collect the empty plate or glass, just set the cheap plastic 16 ounce glass down and walked away. I sipped some more, finished up on email and moved on to the latest news. About 5 minutes later, Waitress breezed by my table and left my bill. $8.34 for the total, I put $20 on the table. I returned to the news and waitress came by again. She say money on the table and asked if I wanted change. I replied "Yes, thank you" and she was off. 5 minutes more, but no waitress and no change. She appeared with an order for another table in the section and I waved her over on her trip back to the kitchen. I asked about my change and she said "I thought you told me to keep it." That was the last straw. I motioned her to come closer, chuckled and quietly told her that I could not seem to justify her tip being larger than the bill I was paying. Her nose, slightly out of joint then, pulled up as she asked me for my copy of the bill. I pulled it out, she picked it up and laid down $11. As she was starting to count change, I told her that was her tip, as that was all I thought her service, presentation and attitude were worth. I thanked her again and left the restaurant. For management/owners of the place, PLEASE put water in glass, not plastic. All of your bar beverages come in glass, as I saw several different beverages served from the bar, so why not give the folks drinking water the same courtesy? 55 minutes from start to finish. This has me curious how they would take care of a road warrior who is eating a full meal with 45 minutes until their flight? After Waitress, there are no other chances.

Went back recently before a movie (drunk movies are the best, remember? Those $8 frozen jack and cokes with half a shot they sell at the theater don't cut it) and they said that they had discontinued the drink. When I asked why, the bartender simply mumbled, "decisions by the owner." The truly annoying part is that all they still had all the ingredients, they just wouldn't make it. Serranos is going around with an overinflated ego of what they really are, which is friendly Tex-Mex, not anything fancier. You have a whopping TWO LOCATIONS, no reason to refuse to give the customer what he wants in the name of chain uniformity, ala Red Lobster & Olive Garden. Anyways, the actual drink they claimed replaced it was not as strong and tasted nasty. I'll take my movie pregaming at Clearivew to Zea's from now on. Oh,the food isn't very good either; they use flour tortillas on everything, including tacos.

I am vegetarian and we had a several of the vegetarian dishes - Bindhi (Okra), Tandoori Vegetables and Aloo Gobi (cauliflower & potatoes). They were fresh and tasty. My feedback is that they could have been spicier - next time I'll remember to ask. I also wish that they served more south Indian dishes. The wait staff was very attentive and helpful.

text: The first time my husband and I went here, I was semi-hungover so I didn't have much tolerance for the extremely slow service. I needed water and food, and quick. Very slow service and when we got our food we were both, "meh" about it. It's hard to screw up breakfast (although I did get the breakfast sandwich on a very small biscuit and ended up having to deconstruct it since it was piled so high). Since I'm always willing to give a place a second shot, we tried it again a few days ago. On a Monday around 12.15 p.m. we sat at our table for 15 minutes before we were even greeted. All 3 of us in our party have worked in the service industry at one time or another so we're pretty patient and understanding if a server is in the weeds. I even told my husband, "If they're busy then I get it, just tell us you'll be right with us and get us a water or something!" Nothing. The host wouldn't make eye contact and there wasn't a manager to be seen. We ended up going to the bar to get our drinks, which took a long time, too, because the bartender automatically made my friend's drink a double and then had to void it out with a manager. We waited about 50 minutes for food, no apologies for the slack service or time of our food. There was no check-back to see how our meals were until our plates were almost cleared. Again, the food was just okay. Definitely not worth the wait. The building is cute and it's convenient for people on the Uptown side of the Quarter or in the CBD. text: Made it to the Vault in Yardley, PA last night. Sampled four beers: Belgium Blonde Ale, Dunkelweisse, American Stout on cask and Coffee Stout on cask. Given the wonderful beers I have had from other local microbreweries I was somewhat disappointed with the beers. There were detectable flaws in the malt, that reminded me of some homebrews. The Dunkelweisse was lacking in flavor, the coffee stout tasted like cold coffee from a Wawa. I thought the American stout was good, and the Belgium blonde ale was very nice. Foodwise the menu is limited but worth sampling. Similar to Tired Hands, the menu is more a small plate chacuterie pizza offering rather than a full menu. I had a "fold" their version of a wrap that is served warm. The sandwich was made with a house made whole wheat flat bread, with imported salami, brie and a fig spread. The fig overwhelmed the brie but overall the combination was a success. The sandwich was served with greens with a balsamic dressing. They use wooden disposable cutlery there and there are no plates, simply cutting boards with brown paper on them. I think this place overall will grow. It certainly is becoming a destination for a night out in Yardley as they have jazz music Thursday Friday and Saturday.

text: I live in the neighborhood and have always enjoyed Bar Ferdinand. I was excited to try out their new menu since David Ansill is now the head chef. Overall, I was pretty disappointed. The Pan con tomate was previously a winner but this time the only tomato we could spot was one or two tomato seeds and it really should be renamed pan sin tomate (which means without) since it was essentially garlic bread. We ordered the Ensalada de Casa which was billed as Bibb lettuce and avocado. Yum!!!! Right?! The salad was dressed nicely however it was a spinach and arugula salad with LITERALLY two-three half Bibb lettuce leaves and two small thin slivers of avocado. Disappointing. We also ordered the squid in ink which was previously a wonderful dish but it was now a salt lick. I wanted to like it so much but we pushed it aside without finishing it since neither of us could stand the salt. The shrimp in garlic had a good garlic flavor but the shrimp were overcooked. It's 2 stars instead of 1 since their dessert still shines. The cider bread & rice pudding are still winners. Overall I'm pretty sad that this neighborhood restaurant is no longer reliable. To the restaurant's credit they took the salad and squid off our bill and offered us dessert on the house. Looks like it will be a dessert only stop.

text: This place is a phenomenal restaurant and it hit me on a sweet spot that reminded me of the nostalgic moments of eating char-grilled korean BBQ at the best restaurants in Korea. I tried 3 dishes: the Thit Nuong Cuon (chargrilled pork rolls), COMBINATION BROKEN RICE, PHO TAI. I know I'm very biased towards this grilling style and I'm absolutely certain many will not agree with this, but I thought that the chargrilling at Vietnam Cafe was done to perfection. The chicken, beef, and pork in my combination broken rice dish was very thinly sliced, lightly marinated, and chargrilled until the edges are slightly burned. This makes the meat extremely crispy on the outer edges. The smell of the lightly burnt meat and marinade brings a flavor you cannot experience with the standard type of grilling methods. This is Asian (korean/vietnamese style) grilling at its finest. The truly amazing thing about this dish was that the meat was relatively moist. The way the chef did this was to cut the meat very thinly at the edges and slightly thicker towards the center which causes the outer edge of the meat pieces to get slightly burnt while making the center parts of the meat relatively moist. Conceptually this is relatively simple, but it is something that is very difficult to execute. Because the meat is so thin, you have a very narrow window to take the meat off the grill. If you overcook it just a TAD BIT then the whole meat becomes extremely tough. This was not the case at Vietnam Cafe. My feelings about the meat were the same for the chargrilled pork rolls. In addition to the meat, the fresh lettuce, the chewy rice vermicelli and the rice wrapping added depth and texture to the taste that was different from the rice dish. In sum, this place absolutely rules with the the broken rice dishes. It was a blessing to have experienced Vietnamese-style chargrilling of this level. As for the pho, I would explore other options. While the Pho shows a very natural flavoring and minimal, if any MSG, I found the noodles to be less chewy and the soup on the blander side compared to Pho specialty shops like Pho75. On a final note, Vietnam Restaurant is extremely clean (they have hand sanitizers and umbrella bags as you enter), has a great decor and a very friendly staff. This restaurant is one of the rare exceptions where great decor goes hand in hand with fantastic food at good prices. I just wish we had such a Vietnamese place in DC =\ 5* for the chargrilled dishes.
label: POS

text: First time today. Close to work. There's actually lots of seating in here, which is not what I deciphered from other reviews. We went early . . . . 11 a.m. Probably four people were already having lunch in there . . . two singles and one couple. I walked around for 15 minutes to get the lay of the land. Where are the soups, where are the premade sandwiches, where is the barbeque? They carry cupcakes by The Cup, Dad's scotch oatmeal cookies and Billy Goat chips . . . supporting the locals. The homemade soups are along the front wall. Today's offerings were chicken noodle, chicken and rice, chicken and dumpling, tomato bisque, lobster bisque, garden vegetable, and broccoli and cheese. You scoop your own. There are three sizes. The premade sandwiches, wraps and salads, along with fruit cups and parfaits are in the cooler case. The salads looked spent. The sandwiches and wraps looked OK, but I just imagined the moisture from the meats oozing into the bread or wrap to make a wilty, soggy mess. Most of the fruit cups proclaimed fresh pineapple was included. Ok. I opted for the Dickey's barbeque. Got a two-meat meal for $10.99. Selected polish sausage and pulled pork. My two sides were green beans with bacon and fried onion tatters (which I had to ask what they are . . . and they're like onion straws). My dining partner got a one-meat meal for $7.99 with two sides. She chose pulled pork, macaroni and cheese, and fried okra. They cook your sides when you order them, so they're not sitting under a heat lamp, or getting lame and limp. We told them we'd never been there before, and the guys on the barbeque side told us everything we needed to know. Very friendly and patient until we were ready to order. I also got a medium size container of the lobster bisque and a medium of the chicken and dumpling soup (totaled $8). Nothing comes with barbeque sauce on it. There are three self-serve sauces you can pick, and they're all heated. One is Dickey's original, one is sweet, one is hot and spicy. Containers and tops are all right there, if you're on a carryout, which we were. Also at that station are the huge whole pickles like the ones you find at the butcher shop in the barrel! I speared two and packed them into my to-go vessel. They're free. Further free, with every order, help yourself to the frozen custard. Cone or cup! Cups have lids, so you can take it to-go. Interestingly, there are two registers. My barbeque meal had to be rung up at one. The soup had to be rung up at the other. Querky! Finally to the food: the polish sausage was moist diagonally cut coins of lucious flavor. The pulled pork was a little dry, but with great flavor. I opted for the Dickey's original barbeque sauce but I'm not much of a sauce person, so I used it sparingly. The green beans with bacon were not green beans . . . they were pole beans. Yes, the bacon was there, but pole beans don't have the same flavor that green beans have -- they're more earthy. The fried onion tatters were a huge portion (lunch by itself), lovely crisp greasiness with great flavor. Dining partner really liked her pulled pork. I tried a bite of her macaroni and cheese. It was creamy cheesy deliciousness (I think it's five-cheese). And she raved about the fried okra. The lobster bisque was quite sweet, very flavorful of lobster, no chunks but little pieces. Nice and creamy. The chicken and dumpling soup was full of plump and lucious dumplings with carrot and celery in a grand thick creamy sauce with beautifully and perfectly diced chicken. Just delicious! No major taste profile here, just comfort food. Both of our meals came with an interesting roll. I don't even know how to describe it . . . rather flat, a little sweet-tasting, dense. I was going to bypass it, but after one taste, I ate the whole thing. Now with all the food I got . . . and for a nearly $20 lunch . . . I brought home enough food for at least three more meals!
label: POS

text: Located next to Arnaud's Restaurant, the French 75 is a cocktail lounge where one can also partake of a limited menu from the main restaurant. It is our favorite traditional cocktail lounge in New Orleans. The décor is very old school and intimate with a 100 year old back bar, cozy settees, classic detailing, and subdued lighting. The bartenders are dressed in crisp white jackets. The bar is presided over by the influential Chris Hannah, whose great skill and flair is only matched by his modesty. Note: Chris helped set up The Museum of the American Cocktail in New Orleans. Over several days, we partook of a broad range of his work: French 75, Sazerac, Rouffignac (which he is credited with reviving), Suissesse (an old drink that has family ties to the Ramos Gin Fizz, but with Herbsaint+absinthe), and La Louisiane. Each was superbly crafted. The service refined and attentive and the clientele seems to appreciate the place and behave accordingly (no obnoxious conventioneers, or self-absorbed hipsters). We met many interesting people at the bar and civil conversation and propriety is definitely a part of the whole scene. We were able to try several dishes from the Bar Menu. Our favorites were the soufflé potatoes (a kind of thin "steak house" cut french fry that puffs up and becomes hollow during frying) with sauce remoulade and, from the main menu, chicken/andouille gumbo. All in all one of the best cocktail experiences we have had in the U.S. It was recently rated one of the top five bars in the country by Esquire Magazine. Note: Afterward, be sure to go upstairs to the Mardi Gras museum.

text: This review is not a complaint. Rather, it is just an effort to share with readers my experience at the East Nashville Branch Post Office on Wednesday, December 19. I hope Postal Service workers and the residents of East Nashville might get some profit from the perspective of a loyal customer. On Friday, December 14, my wife and I turned in a yellow card requesting that our mail be placed on hold for three days, December 17 - 19. We were traveling during that time but arrived back in Nashville around mid-day on the 19th which was earlier than we had anticipated getting home. As we drove toward our home, I stopped at the Post Office to pick up my mail. The yellow "hold card" clearly said that I would pick up my mail at the end of the hold. I drove into the parking area. There was one space available. It was next to a beautiful bronze-colored truck that belongs to a nice woman who works at the window in the Post Office. I see the truck parked in that space often. Often when I come to the Post Office I also see cars that are parked outside of the marked lines which often means that one car takes up two spaces. Although there was a car on the line to the left of the available space, I was able to park my car CLEARLY WITHIN THE LINES OF THE SPACE. Nevertheless, it was very close to the bronze truck on my right. The truck is very big and my car is pretty large also. As I was walking toward the front doors of the Post Office, two ladies in the parking area were having a mild argument because one of the persons had banged her car door up against the car in the space next to hers. But it is Christmas time, the spaces are lined way too small for cars, and so the argument ended quickly. I went into the Post Office and found not surprisingly that I was third in line OUTSIDE THE DOOR. So there must have been 10 people, more or less, in front of me. Now I understand that. December 19th is one of the busiest days of the year for the Post Office. All three windows were operating and the postal workers were doing the best they could to move customers along. I had to wait a good long time to get served. But I certainly was friendly and did not show an "attitude" since everyone was doing the best they could to service all the customers. When I finally got to a window, I gave the worker my address and an ID and asked for my mail. He went to the back and was gone a very long time. I am sure he was trying to find my mail. Eventually, he returned with just two pieces of mail. I told him that something was amiss but that I would take those two pieces and try to figure out what was going on. When I got out to my car, I found the nice lady with the lovely bronze pickup truck waiting impatiently and with a face full of attitude because she was unable to get to the driver's side of her truck in the small space that was between my car and her vehicle. Let me say again, MY CAR WAS WITHIN THE LINES. If there is a problem, it is caused by the size of her truck, the size of my car, the limited number of parking spaces, and most importantly, the fact that the spaces are lined too small to accommodate cars with a reasonable space in between. I apologized but the nice lady would not say a word and just kept giving me a face full of attitude. So I drove on home. And, to top off my day at the Post Office, I discovered that our mail carrier was in the process of delivering mail to our home. And, worse, he had delivered mail for the two previous days. Thus, our mail was never put on hold. The two pieces of mail that I got at the Post Office were actually scheduled to go out with the carrier the next day, Thursday. So, what does all this mean? Christmas time can be frustrating. Everyone needs to be patient and understanding. As for the big beautiful bronze truck, I am afraid if the nice lady keeps parking it in that space, it is going to be horribly dinged up with careless parkers who bang their doors up against their neighbor's vehicles. I also might suggest that should funding ever be available, the lines on the customer parking spaces need to be redone so as to provide wider spaces. But, given how Congress misuses the USPS budget, I doubt if that will happen anytime soon. Best wishes for the season and lets all hope for less frustration and more peace and goodwill among us all. Sincerely, Jim Brooks 1813 Woodland St Nashville, TN

Before I go into my review of the cupcakes themselves, I have to comment on the name and their logo. Spelling a word differently because it's 'trendy' does not appeal to me. I don't understand why cupcake has to be spelled with a 'k'. This is just wrong and teaches kids to misspell words. In addition to the spelling, I hate their font choice for their logo. Being friends with people in the production/design world, they have taught me all about the dos/don'ts of fonts and design. Unfortunately, the Kupcake Factory font reminds me of the font Curlz. I cringe having to even write this word. Enough of my rant on their logo choice, I will move on to my assessment of the cupcakes. Having tried their cupcakes on numerous occasions, I think that the cupcakes are 'meh' to average at best. Their cupcakes are a little dry for my preference. The service is just average, and the store is a little drab and empty. They have pictures of cupcakes on their walls, but I don't even think the pictures are of their own cupcakes. The cupcakes cost about $2.50/cupcake, so they are cheaper than Bee Sweet's. Personally, I would rather have Bee Sweet's cupcakes or even Cochon Butcher. Hell, I feel as though I can bake a better cupcake with a box recipe if I had the time and effort. I'm no cupcake expert, but I think that the Kupcake Factory should re-brand themselves and revamp their recipe.

text: Range is one of the newer additions to downtown, and once again, the folks behind places like Bailey's Chocolate Bar, Bridge, and Rooster hit it out of the park. They are my favorite restaurateurs in the downtown STL area - even though each place is very different in niche, cuisine, hours, decor, each has the impression of being well thought-through for what it is. So, what Range is - a modern update of the soda bar / roller-skate-wearing carhop burger joints of yore. No, you don't pull up in your car and get served by comely ladies in skates, but the food is pure americana: burgers, fries, shakes, and floats. Except did we mention: *boozy* shakes and *boozy* floats? Yes. I would put on my bobby socks for these. The interior is dominated by a large bar-height table that runs the length of the restaurant, with stools for seating (we should add: there is also a bar-height bar that runs the length of the restaurant, parallel to the table ;-). Perhaps a bit off-putting to the standard middle-american diner, who seems to prefer maintaining a certain distance from (gasp!) other people, but we found it charming. Came in on a super-busy Friday night but nonetheless had maybe a 10 minute wait for a spot for 2 (which was just right for ordering drinks at the bar). The burger menu includes many inventive takes on the classic, and it seems you can substitute different kinds of patties (pork, chicken, bison, lamb, veggie) for the free-range cow patties if you so desire (some burgers appear to be crafted around the type of meat involved, so sub at your own risk). We went exotic with the PB&J (Bison with arugula Pesto, goat cheese, and tomato jam) and the smoking duck burgers - the former was just... do it. You will not be sad. The duck was OK - nothing wrong with it, but in comparison to the PB&J it was a little boring. You should just order two sides of fries rather than one large - costs less, plus you get to try more sauces. The rooster is the same spicy/creamy sauce served on top of the crepes at the Rooster, and the homemade catsup was just fine. Haven't tried the others yet. The big winner, though, is the boozy horchata milkshake: an invention that should have come to be long before now. You will somehow make room for it, we promise. They have a fun Survivor-style competition where each week, two burgers "face off" in a battle - the one that gets ordered more gets to stay on the menu. Should keep things interesting over time - great idea for nom longevity.

text: I really would like to support my local independently owned bike shop, but the people there are condescending, always try to sell me more work than I need on my bike, and despite what everyone says, are more expensive for repairs than the bigger bike shops I've gone to. I rode out to Human Zoom because my boyfriend and I had stopped in there once when he had a problem with his bike on the Schuylkill River Trail. It was a Sunday and they weren't actually open yet, but they opened up very quickly and took us right away. I knew the people there were friendly and I knew they sold Treks, so they were likely to have parts if I needed them. I went in on a Friday afternoon around 3 or 4 PM, when there was only one other person in the store. I just bought my first road bike (after riding a hybrid for years), a 2010 Women's Trek, off craigslist and wanted to get the bike checked out. The mechanic spent a long time with the bike going over everything, made some adjustments, and fixed the seat that was installed improperly - all free of charge. Then he spent a while going over the bike with me and explaining things about the gears that I never would have figured out on my own (like how the second front gear has two positions, and that I should avoid riding with the gears in positions that stretch the chain). He also explained some of the differences between fancier road bikes that only have two front gears and mine with three front gears and 9 back gears, which assured me that this is the right bike for me as a beginner. He left the handle bars in the highest position which he said will be the most comfortable for me as a beginner, but he explained that as I get more comfortable with the bike I can have the handle bars lowered for more power. I was really impressed how much time he spent going over with me how the bike works and what i need to know to ride it and do to maintain it. Then he sold me two sea foam green bottle cages that match my bike almost perfectly (and put them on for me), and an extra tube to keep with me in case I get a flat. The bottle cages were $20 each, which is more than I would typically spend on something like that, but they look awesome, and the tube was $10. I did not feel pressured at all to buy anything or have any unnecessary work done on my bike. Even when I asked them about getting a new seat for the bike, they encouraged me to wait until I was more comfortable riding a road bike before determining that the seat was really too narrow or too hard. They did encourage me to get padded shorts, but didn't insist on getting them there. Overall I had a really great experience at Human Zoom. I highly recommend them and hope everyone else has an equally good experience there :) One other plus is that they have a pump in their vestibule if you ever need air when you're on the trail, and they have bike racks set up in the vestibule and in the shop to store your bike when you're in the shop or want to run into a nearby store.

Like many of the local neighborhood markets in Latin America and the Caribbean, Cacciatore's is well stocked with deli foods, extremely fresh produce, pastries, beans, rices, pastas, sauces and seasonings. Add to that shelves filled with countless boxed and canned goods, coolers of beer and sodas, and homemade spice blends. In addition Cacciatore's has a full wine shop, and a huge butcher shop / meat counter extending along two sides of the store with freshly sliced cheese, cold cuts, homemade sausages, and a fantastic selection of custom-cut steaks, beef, chicken, pork, seafood and fish. I have been here several times, and every time I went the food was consistently fresh and tasty no matter what I ordered. The entrees that I usually get here are the calamari, Manhattan chowder (which is tomato-based), mixed seafood grill, and/or seafood croquette (which is like a crab cake). The fish is also pretty good as well (like the salmon in Coca-cola glaze or mahi-mahi), but it is somewhat pricey. However, it is worth every cent because it is fresh (and I noticed that every time I come here, it does get crowded quickly). Also, the atmosphere of the restaurant has a rustic but modern feel, complete with a full bar and aquarium (don't worry, it's the kind where the fish inside it is too small to eat). The service is prompt and friendly too. My only complaint is that the parking near here, while there is plenty of it, can be hard to access if you're not from the area. There's one lot where you might have to pay (it's right next to an Amtrak station), and there's a free (but time-limited) lot as well. So, if you are looking for a place to eat some great, fresh seafood, go to Enterprise Fish Co. However, if your wallet feels pinched by high prices there, go during lunch or happy hour instead.

We figured we'd stop in as the brewery is in Lambertville, and walk over the bridge into New Hope for the day. When we arrived it was around a quarter to 2pm, and just in time for their 2pm tour. When you walk into the front door of the brewery, you end up in their tasting room. A lot of people were there that day but we made our way to the bar and ordered the $1 4 beer sampler, which was a great deal. My favorite beer on tap that day was the seasonal "Hippo-Lantern" beer (a Pumpkin beer). The tour began a few minutes after 2pm and, is free, in case you were wondering though of course I'm sure donations/tips at the bar are appreciated. The location is small so the tour does not last long, but you do learn some interesting facts about beer if you are into that. My husband and I are very much into craft beer so we enjoyed the information. I was surprised to know that they are only a 10 person company, wow. The company is doing so well that they are outgrowing their current location. At the end of your tour you can go back to the tasting room and bring home a six pack if you'd like. They also sell t-shirts. All in all an interesting experience and again if you are a beer enthusiast it's definitely worth a trip. If it's a nice day, you can hop on over to New Hope and explore all the shops and restaurants they have to offer as well.

text: Still searching for a spot to get good seafood with good service in Midcity, I recently tried Liuzza's. After spending way too much time trying to decipher the incomprehensible menu (chose a typeface, font size and justification, for the love of God!), my roommate and I decided to start with a heap of onion rings -- which were well cut and well fried, though dip-less and completely unseasoned. Come time to order our entrees, having a hankerin', I opted for the fried catfish plate. The waitress told me to choose a side, so I took out my Rosetta stone and had anther look at the menu. From the jumbled list of sides I picked jambalaya. My catfish was battered in the same floury, spice-less batter as the onion rings (my hankerin' was hoping for a good, crisp cornmeal dredge). The filets were perfectly cooked but almost inedibly bland until I tracked down a waitress and asked for some Tony's. After dusting it generously with seasoning salt, it was actually pretty good! Leading me to wonder... How is it that a New Orleans neighborhood "institution" doesn't know how to season fish?? I could have forgiven the rest, but when our handwritten, chicken scratch (utterly indecipherable) bill came, we learned that the mushy side of jambalaya that I barely touched was an additional $4. If the menu were legible and I had known that, I would have gotten something else. Adding all that to halfhearted service that toed the line of being outright terrible and the fact that credit cards aren't accepted and there is a $2.50 surcharge at the ATM, I don't see any reason to ever return to Liuzza's, even in the most dire Midcity seafood pinch.

text: I just came back from a disenchanting dinner at Lee How Fook. My boyfriend wanted to take me there for a while and hyped it up as not being your typical chinese from the place down the street- meaning fresher ingredients and I assumed a more delicious taste. The ingredients did taste fresh, but this is the only time I can remember thinking fresh ingredients had a "funny" taste to them. Everything seemed to have an off/odd flavor..kind of like when something is made with bad oil. Due to the hype and my boyfriend's appetite, I feel comfortable saying I sampled a fair share of the menu to determine whether I would eat there again. We had pan seared dumplings, which I didn't like at all becuase there was such an unappealing oil flavor. Wonton Soup, spring rolls, General Tso's Chicken and Yan Chow Fried Rice. The wrappers on the wontons in the soup were very thin and layered and the pork inside a very light color. The general tso's had to be the worst I've ever had, which is funny since I only ordered it because I thought it was a safe bet. It had a horrible flavor and the texture was even worse. My boyfriend didn't like it at all either, so we ended up sharing his Yan Chow rice. I liked the rice, actually, a lot but wished they would have cleaned the shrimp. The service really wasn't great- or even good for the matter of fact. Things were dropped on the table and forcefully arranged, my fork taken and not returned. There were a lot of people "working" there but no one seemed to be paying much attention to the guests. I'm not a raving chinese food fan, but good chinese is good chinese. I found it very strange that I found very little of what I ate there actually good based on all of the hype and awards they've won.

text: I came to Lenny's with high hopes based on these Yelp reviews. My experience has left me feeling "meh." I brought two pairs of boots in. text: While I am no authority on Persian cuisine, this place has good food with a good price. First off, this place is definitely meat-heavy; very little vegetarian dishes seem available. There is also a nearly 50% price difference between lunch and dinner meals-visit for lunch and order the junior dishes; the meal is definitely large enough. I ordered a junior chicken shank with a chicken kabob and lamb shank. Ambiance is nice casual cross between a sports bar and a diner. Service was friendly. While we waited for the order to arrive, "sabzi" was brought over-a medley of parsley and butter, with a naan-like bread. While not great, it was not bad either. The main course was great. The chicken had a nice charbroiled taste with a lot of juices, while the lamb shank pervaded with spices and was delightfully crumbly, easily coming off the bone-it reminded me of a meat stew with it texture and rich aroma. The rice was as tasteful as any other rice dish, though it did serve up to sop up the juices from the lamb and chicken. The Shirazi was not particularly good; the tomato, cucumbers, and onion had obviously been chilled for a while and lost its taste and texture. It could have been done better. Still, the whole course cost around $10, a nice deal for a nice meal. I will come back.
